short: The caller that starts an operation and waits for its result.
detail: One original operation can produce several attempts if the client retries. The client deadline covers all those attempts.
design: Count client operations separately from server attempts so retry success does not hide added load.

short: The number of new client operations offered per second, before retries.
detail: The load generator here keeps sending at its configured rate even while earlier requests wait. Manual sends and bursts add to that load.
design: Test offered load independently of response time. A generator that waits for responses can conceal overload by slowing itself down.

short: An operation served on a particular route, such as `/b` or `/c`.
detail: Each route here calls a different dependency. The routes can share workers or reserve separate pools.
design: Measure reliability per operation. Healthy aggregate metrics can hide failure on a lower-volume route.

short: A downstream service whose response is needed to complete a request.
detail: B can take 50 ms or 2 s, return 503s, or hang. C consistently takes 50 ms.
design: Map shared resources across the dependency graph to see where a failure may spread beyond direct callers.

short: The slots A uses to process concurrent requests.
detail: A slot remains occupied while waiting for a dependency. In this model it also stays occupied during a retry delay inside A.
design: Size the pool for the time a request holds its slot, including I/O waits. An async implementation still needs limits on in-flight work.

short: Accepted requests wait here until a worker is available.
detail: Requests dispatch in arrival order within each pool. Queue depth counts waiting requests and excludes those in worker slots.
design: Set queue bounds from acceptable waiting time and service capacity. A larger buffer can make more responses arrive too late to be useful.

short: A duration after which a caller stops waiting for a response.
detail: A starts its invocation timeout when the request reaches it, so queueing and retries at A spend the same time. A reports a failure and releases the slot when that timer expires.
design: Bound waits wherever they hold scarce resources. Choose limits using healthy tail latency and the response time the client can use.

short: The point in time after which the caller can no longer use a response.
detail: A relative timeout produces a deadline when it starts. The client here keeps the same deadline across all retries. An already-running invocation can outlive its client.
design: Use the remaining deadline to decide whether there is time for another attempt. Propagate cancellation where downstream work can actually stop.

short: The time available for queueing, work, and returning a response before the client deadline.
detail: Leave room for transit and response handling. Several downstream calls or retries may need to share one invocation budget.
design: Give the inner operation a shorter limit than the outer one so the outer caller has time to act on the result.

short: All eligible worker slots are occupied, so new requests have to wait or be rejected.
detail: Slow dependencies can exhaust a pool at low CPU use because each wait holds a slot longer. Caller abandonment does not automatically release the slot.
design: Watch active slots and queue age alongside CPU to identify which resource is preventing progress.

short: A failure spreads when one part of the system consumes resources that another part needs.
detail: Slow calls to B take all of A’s slots. Calls to healthy C now wait in A, even though C itself could serve them.
design: Look for shared queues, executors, sockets, and storage when deciding where to put isolation boundaries.

short: A new attempt at an operation after an earlier attempt failed or ran out of time.
detail: Three attempts includes the original attempt plus up to two retries. This lab retries eligible B failures only while there is time left.
design: Retry transient failures only when the operation is safe to replay and another attempt has a plausible chance of helping.

short: Retries produce more dependency calls than the original client workload.
detail: If the client tries A up to three times and A tries B up to three times per invocation, one original operation can make nine B calls.
design: Assign retry ownership deliberately. Compare downstream attempts to original requests and inspect the worst case along the full call path.

short: A retry delay that grows by a fixed multiplier after each failure.
detail: The fixed delays here are 100 ms then 200 ms at each retry layer. Requests that fail together can still retry together.
design: Place a cap on delay and respect the remaining deadline. Use jitter when many callers can see the same failure.

short: Random variation in retry timing that spreads requests out.
detail: Full jitter draws a fresh uniform delay between zero and the current backoff cap. The cap doubles after another failure.
design: Use jitter to reduce peaks after correlated failure. Pair it with a retry budget to limit total extra work.

short: A surge of repeat attempts that overwhelms a dependency or makes an outage worse.
detail: Fast failures leave more time for retries to be issued. Correlated failures send many callers back to the same dependency at once.
design: Measure first attempts and retries separately at both short and long intervals to expose sharp bursts hidden by averages.

short: A failure that sustains itself after its initial trigger disappears.
detail: In this lab, excess attempts make B return fast 503s. Those errors produce retries that can keep B over its recovery limit after the injected fault ends.
design: Plan how to interrupt the feedback loop during an incident. Recovery may need temporarily lower traffic than steady-state operation.

short: A cap on repeat attempts relative to original work.
detail: Here, ten first B attempts earn one extra attempt shared across layers. The budget starts empty when enabled and can bank at most two retries.
design: Tie retries to normal volume, bound burst credit, and make the scope explicit. Independent budgets at several layers may still amplify load.

short: Repeating the same operation has the same intended effect as applying it once.
detail: A stable idempotency key can make a write safe to retry if the server durably links the key to the effect and result. A response can fail after the write committed.
design: Define replay semantics before adding automatic retries. Keep deduplication records for at least the supported retry horizon.

short: An admission policy that stops calling a failing dependency and tests it before resuming.
detail: The circuit starts closed. Enough recent failures open it, and after a cool-down it moves half-open to check actual calls.
design: Scope the breaker to the dependency or operation with a shared failure mode. C stays independent when B’s breaker opens.

short: Normal requests are allowed through the circuit to B.
detail: Completed B calls contribute to a rolling failure rate. The model needs six observations before it can trip.
design: Minimum sample counts help a breaker avoid overreacting to sparse traffic. A low-volume service may need a longer window.

short: Requests bypass B while the breaker waits out its cool-down.
detail: A returns either an immediate error or a fallback. In this model, calls already in flight finish under their original time limits.
design: Distinguish circuit bypasses from dependency failures in telemetry. An open breaker drastically changes the population reaching B.

short: The breaker lets a small number of real requests test whether B has recovered.
detail: This lab allows a single trial in flight. Two consecutive trial successes close the circuit and a failed trial reopens it.
design: Bound probe concurrency to avoid swamping a recovering service. Use probes that reflect real work and observe their success separately.

short: A recent interval that advances with the current time.
detail: When a B result arrives in the closed state, only results newer than the window cutoff count. A wider window retains more history.
design: Use enough history for a reliable decision while keeping the window short enough to detect faults at the required speed.

short: The failure percentage that opens a closed circuit once it has enough observations.
detail: 503s and B timeouts count as failures. Local queue expiry, fallback responses, and calls bypassed by the breaker are excluded.
design: Separate faults the dependency can influence from local admission and validation errors. A noisy signal can trip a healthy dependency.

short: How long the circuit stays open before it allows a trial.
detail: Every trip starts a fresh cool-down. Elapsed time permits a trial and leaves recovery to the trial result.
design: Choose a duration that gives the dependency room to recover while limiting how long healthy capacity can go unused.

short: A reduced response A can return when it bypasses B.
detail: The lab models a local cached fallback with no dependency call. It counts as a response but is excluded from full successes and goodput.
design: Define what stale or partial data is safe to serve and expose fallback usage. An expensive fallback can become the next overloaded dependency.

short: A separate resource allocation that limits where a failure can spread.
detail: Here, each route gets its own waiting lane and half of A’s slots. Idle C slots cannot be borrowed by B.
design: Reserve capacity for critical operations and check for shared bottlenecks beneath the split, including CPU and connection limits.

short: Rejecting new work early when there is too much already waiting or running.
detail: The model returns an early 503 if no eligible worker is idle and the waiting queue is at its cap. A shed request never starts a dependency call.
design: Set admission limits from latency and useful completions. Make upstream callers treat rejection as a capacity signal to avoid feeding a retry storm.

short: The rate of useful results delivered to clients.
detail: For this lab, a full response arriving within 250 ms counts. Late successes, degraded responses, and failures are excluded.
design: Define useful in terms of the user objective and inspect goodput under overload. A high volume of quick errors can inflate throughput.

short: The rate of operations completing per unit of time.
detail: This chart counts terminal client outcomes per second, including errors, fallback responses, and deadline expiry. It counts an original once regardless of its attempts.
design: Label what the rate measures. Client outcomes, successful work, and dependency attempts are different populations.

short: The latency at or below which half of the measured requests finished.
detail: This is a nearest-rank median on full responses in each one-second sample. The chart shows a gap if there were no full responses.
design: Use the median for typical performance and pair it with a tail percentile and outcome rates to spot the slow or missing minority.

short: The latency at or below which 99% of the measured requests finished.
detail: This chart uses only full responses in each one-second sample. At low sample counts nearest-rank p99 is close to the maximum.
design: Evaluate tail latency alongside availability. Fast rejection and dropped requests can make the measured latency look better while the service gets worse.

short: The fraction of completed client operations that ended in error.
detail: Errors include shedding, definitive dependency failure, and timeout. Fallback responses count separately as degraded outcomes.
design: Report error and fallback rates beside latency and goodput. A latency percentile cannot account for outcomes absent from its sample.

short: An admission limit that changes as measured service capacity changes.
detail: Some controllers infer saturation from rising latency and lower the number of concurrent requests they admit. This lab uses fixed limits.
design: Treat the controller as its own feedback loop. Set bounds, measure per route where needed, and test that a change in request mix does not cause instability.

short: A controller raises a limit gradually and reduces it proportionally when it detects congestion.
detail: An example adds one slot when conditions are healthy and removes half on a congestion signal. The signal and update interval affect stability.
design: Use a credible congestion measurement and leave time to observe each adjustment. Many independent controllers can otherwise oscillate together.

short: Preserving useful behavior while reducing what the system promises during a fault.
detail: A can keep C available while B fails, or return a clearly marked cached fallback for B. A reduced response can have its own user-facing target.
design: Decide which features and data can degrade before an incident. Give the reduced mode independent capacity and measurements.

short: A probe of whether a component is running or able to serve work.
detail: A process can pass a liveness probe while real queries fail. The breaker here tests real B requests in half-open state.
design: Pick a probe that answers the decision at hand. Changing routing based on shallow success can send traffic back before critical work is ready.

short: A response saying the server is temporarily unable to handle the request.
detail: Here B may reply 503 under a fault or overload, and A uses 503 when it sheds work. An upstream client may see the same status for different causes.
design: Document how overload responses should be handled. Retry-After or equivalent hints help only if callers honor them within their budgets.

short: More work arrives than the service can handle at its target quality.
detail: This retry scenario models B overload as more than 12 starts over 250 ms and recovery at four or fewer. The gap between those thresholds represents reduced capacity during recovery.
design: Find the limiting resource and test recovery under traffic as well as initial saturation. Stop adding work once useful throughput falls.
